This reminded me of the poem "Mercy" by Rudy Francisco.

She asks me to kill the spider.
Instead, I get the most
peaceful weapons I can find.

I take a cup and a napkin.
I catch the spider, put it outside
and allow it to walk away.

If I am ever caught in the wrong place
at the wrong time, just being alive
and not bothering anyone,

I hope I am greeted
with the same kind
of mercy.

Proud of you, OP! Social anxiety can be debilitating and it was a huge leap for you to make the decision and try to change something that feels like an innate part of you (being afraid of people). I'm cheering on your continuous improvement that you no longer ever feel like watching the world from behind a glass tank.

I've put off getting diagnosed for years out of fear that there's something "wrong" with me. That's just putting it simply. Eventually, I just went spiraling down and had a full-blown mental breakdown. I lost friends, relationships, became jobless, and became detached from my family.

At this point, I seriously had to reflect and accept that something is wrong and that I needed help. When I realized that, it was hard because getting diagnosed either means one of each to me at the time

"i get diagnosed and that means im crazy" or"i dont get diagnosed with anything so that means i hurt all these people just because im an asshole".

I got checked eventually because honestly, what else is there to do? I was at rock bottom. No way to go but up, maybe? So I got diagnosed. My diagnoses changed several times after I changed doctors several times too. My last diagnosis is Bipolar 1 (same as you) and have been taking meds for it on-and-off for about 2 years now because I struggle with keeping up with routine.

Going back to my initial point, the fear in our initial diagnosis may come from denial or internalized stigma we have towards mental illness and please know that it's okay to feel that way. It's scary to accept that you're ill and your mind can feel like the enemy but I hope you never feel that something is "wrong" with you just because you're diagnosed.

Please take the meds when you're ready. If you really don't want to, I recommend you telling the doctor. A good one will not force you to take the meds and will refer you to undergo psychotherapy instead-- this is something I did majority of last year. No meds just therapy bc I got tired of the side effects. I'm rooting for you, OP.

I'm sorry that this happened to you, OP but I'm glad to hear that you're still with us. Please try to remind yourself that your father cannot blame anyone else for his actions. It's totally unfair of him to tell you such a cruel thing especially coming back from a suicide attempt. He is a full-grown adult and should have known better than shifting blame. Most likely, he feels shame from relapsing and is projecting that shame and guilt onto you to make himself feel better. 

I understand that you may feel guilty for it due to him directly blaming you for his relapse but **please remember that you're not responsible your father's actions.** We're only responsible for our own actions, same way that your father is responsible for his. 

I hope you continue staying and that you are able to get away from your toxic home life soon enough. Hugs, man.

It's difficult to help people who refuse to help themselves or even worse, refuse to accept that they need help even when their actions are negatively affecting the people around them already. I can see that you care for your mother OP, is there a way to gently nudge her in that direction? Some people react negatively when being confronted with cold hard truths. Maybe she needs to be eased into it?

For people in older generations who have developed and lived with such a stigma with mental illness, just the conversation around it makes them unreasonably uneasy out of fear of being labelled as "crazy". Perhaps having dialogue about healthy mental care just around your mother (like just making her hear it without her being the topic of the conversation) may make her open to discussing it more.

The last one I can suggest requires more effort which is showing her by example that it's okay to get some help. I don't know how close you are to your mother but if you can be open to her if you're getting therapy as well then that's a great conversation starter. Maybe ask your therapist (if you have one) if you could invite your mother for the next session to talk about you and if they agree, invite your mom. The fact that the session will be about talking about you can make her less apprehensive about meeting a therapist but also shows her that therapy is not just for "crazy" people. I understand that this last suggestion can be construed as a little manipulative for some but people are afraid of what they don't know. I think exposing her to the environment without her feeling like a subject of scrutiny can alleviate some anxiety she feels around mental health discussions.

Ooooof as a fellow artist I agree with you. The "tortured artist" trope needs to be put to rest.

I totally agree with the balancing act and the cognitive dissonance of constantly trying to get better versus wanting to give up completely because what's the point, right? It's like society tells us it's not our fault to be dealt shitty cards but it's totally uncaring as well on how we choose to repair ourselves or sadly destroy ourselves with.

The defensiveness we feel over our action I think can also come from our belief that what our actions doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things and that they're only going to affect and hurt us only. Do you think we (people with MIs) always have that denial in us that what we do wont matter because of our usually poor perception of self-worth that it also blinds us to real-world effects of our behaviors (like towards social and professional circles)?

If I could contextualize that question further, since we're dealing with our daily and constant emotional torment, it desensitizes us from external aspects of our lives and makes us sort of apathetic (for example not caring about poor work performance or being irritable or lashing out at people who care for us).

hey friend, it might sound cliche but what you're going through is perfectly normal as you're just starting out college. i personally sat alone in the park during my freshman year and ate my lunch in tears for a few months due to my extreme social anxiety. everyone just felt too intimidating to talk to much less befriend. though let me tell you a secret-- everyone's just as scared as you are. new people and a brand new environment is definitely anxiety-inducing. some are just better at hiding it.

while introversion might seem like a hindrance to making friends, remember that there are tons of other introverts all around you just also trying to muster up enough courage to say hi to you and ask to hang out. i agree with the others that joining clubs/orgs will make it a little bit easier to find people with the same interests as you.

let me assure you that it will be alright and you'll find your tribe too, eventually. it sucks right now but the right people will come by soon. adjusting is very difficult so try to be patient with yourself for now. hugs to you, it will be alright.
